messages.author: 39971e2c19b8ec70
messages.subject: Integrated Population Model - terminology
parts:
Hello everyone,

I just constructed a model (modification of Jolly Seber) which models
everything - population growth, survival and recruitment. It is from a
single data source - Constant Effort Sites ringing scheme and I am
about to publish it. Now I wonder: is such a model classified as an
Integrated Population Model?

What precisely the "Integrated" means in this term?

1) Does it mean that more data sets are integrated in one model?

or

2) Does it mean that all demographic information is integrated into
single, complete and comprehensive population equation (N[t] = some
function of N[t-1]) including all demographic parameters?

My model clearly does not comply with 1, since it is only from single
data source, but it does comply with 2 - it does integrate all
information possible. So, I now need to know if I should present my
model as IPM or something else.

Thanks a lot!

Tomas

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Integrated Population Model - terminology
parts:
Hi Tomas,

This is an interesting discussion.  I would say that you need at least 1 other data source that provides information on a population process for it to be an IPM, even if those data come from the same population (same individuals even).  This would distinguish an individual attribute like body size from something like litter size (# offspring) -- the former can be incorporated into capture-recapture but does not necessarily inform a population process like the latter does.

Just my debatable opinion of course, interested to see what others think.

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: Integrated Population Model - terminology
parts:
Dear Tomas, and hello Dan,

of course, 'integrated' is just a buzz-word, some might say. However, the way the term has come to be used in the literature in the context of IPMs, it is exactly what Dan says: you need at least two different data sources. And what's more, my colleague Michael Schaub (e.g., in the Review paper with Fitsum Abadie, around 2011) defines integrated population models as population models that are fit to at least two types of independent data sources: one of which must be a time series of population counts and the other one a data set that more directly informs about demographic rates such as survival, e.g., a capture-recapture data set.

In a more general sense, we can recognize that 'integrated models' are one of the main developmental branches of all of ecological statistics: the field is FULL with new models where people find a model-based way of combining different data sets that inform on the same underlying process. In the context of hierarchical models, this almost always means that there is a shared process model, but different observation models for the different data sets.

Best regards ---- Marc
